clue.text: Rental mishaps spoilt ideal social system

indicators.note: something spoilt has been ruined and knocked out of its proper shape, so the letters before it are rearranged

parts.note: both words taken as written, all thirteen letters used

explanation.surface: A landlord's run of bad luck with lettings wrecks somebody's utopian dream.
explanation.walkthrough: PHALANSTERISM is Fourier's scheme of people living in self-supporting communes called phalansteries.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Fourier proposed the phalanstery as a utopian commune, so his system was an idealised plan for organising society.

clue.text: Garden plants? Nasty disease enveloping odd ones in Hull

indicators.note: to envelop is to wrap round, so the disease goes around the kept letters

parts.note: the pox is a nasty disease; its first two letters open the wrapper

indicators.note: the odd ones are the first, third and so on, so only those positions of the word that follows are kept

parts.note: Hull is the Yorkshire port; its first and third letters
the last letter of the pox closes the wrapper

explanation.surface: A gardener in Hull finds the beds attacked by some horrible blight.
explanation.walkthrough: The disease POX opens round the odd letters of Hull: P(HL)OX. The question mark admits that the plant name works as a plural here.
explanation.definitionFit: Phlox is a genus of garden flowers grown for their scented clusters, and the name serves for many plants.

clue.text: Your WI oddly appearing in dress as a caterpillar? (11, two words)

indicators.note: the scrambled letters show up within the garment word

parts.note: a habit is a form of dress, as worn by monks or for riding

indicators.note: oddly suggests the letters behave strangely, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Women's Institute member turns up in fancy dress as a creepy-crawly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' looks like a signal to take alternate letters; here it scrambles all of them. The WI is the Women's Institute, a British village women's club.
explanation.definitionFit: Hairy woubit is a dialect name in Chambers for a hairy caterpillar, such as that of the tiger moth.

clue.text: E.g. garter, as in elevated count

indicators.note: the word for 'as' goes inside the raised word
in a down clue, elevated means the word is written upwards, so read backwards

parts.note: to tell is to count, as a bank teller does
e.g. (for example) can stand for 'as', as in 'such as'

explanation.surface: A garter offered as an example, tucked into some lofty tally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'E.g.' belongs to the definition, while 'as' supplies the abbreviation for 'for example'.
explanation.definitionFit: A leglet is a band or ornament worn around the leg, and a garter is one such band.

clue.text: From Chesterfield perhaps, last achieving dominance? (4, two words)

indicators.note: the final letter takes the top spot, so it moves from the end to the front of the word

parts.note: a chesterfield is a padded leather sofa; 'perhaps' marks it as one example

explanation.surface: A query about whether some report came from the Derbyshire town of Chesterfield, which finally topped the table.
explanation.walkthrough: Chesterfield looks like the town; it is the sofa. Moving its last letter to the front gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: As of introduces the date something starts, as in 'as of Monday', meaning from that time onward.

clue.text: Trooper abroad in due course joining conflict

parts.note: so in the sense 'and then', as in 'and so to bed', marking what comes next in time
war is armed conflict

explanation.surface: A soldier serving overseas expects eventually to be sent into battle.
explanation.definitionFit: A sowar was a mounted soldier in the Indian army, so a cavalry trooper serving far from Britain.

clue.text: Two Canadian bucks? Front of hoof is round on one

indicators.note: something that is round another encircles it, so the front of the hoof wraps the other pieces

parts.note: the toe is the front part of a hoof; its first two letters
taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Two male deer in Canada, one with a hoof that is round at the front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bucks' looks like deer to suit the hoof, but it is North American slang for dollars; the toe of a hoof is its front part.
explanation.definitionFit: The toonie is Canada's two-dollar coin, and buck is everyday North American slang for a dollar.

clue.text: Many a series turning up includes this repeat

indicators.note: in a down clue, something turning up reads from the bottom of the column, so its letters run backwards
the words before it include the answer within their run of letters, spanning the word break

parts.note: the last letter of the first word, the whole second word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A grumble about television: countless series contain a rerun.
explanation.definitionFit: To resay something is to say it again, so the word means to repeat.

clue.text: Old jade I abandoned stole pennies at random

indicators.note: letters placed at random follow no order, so what remains is shuffled
once I is abandoned it is left behind, so that one letter drops out of the phrase

parts.note: both words taken as written

explanation.surface: An old nag, or a disreputable old woman, made off with some coins without the speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old jade' looks like a worn-out horse or woman, but it is the green stone; the word I comes out of the phrase before it is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Spleenstone is an obsolete name for jade, which was once believed to cure ailments of the spleen.

clue.text: Sweetened wine, once a source of inspiration when penning line

indicators.note: penning something means shutting it in, as sheep in a pen, so the inspiration encloses the line

parts.note: a muse inspires poets; its first two letters
L is the standard abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A poet recalls a sweet wine that once inspired whatever lines were being written.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penning' looks like writing to suit the poet's muse, but here it means enclosing.
explanation.definitionFit: Mulse was a drink of wine boiled with honey, a sweetened wine of classical times, now archaic.

clue.text: Wild flower speeds section of verse

parts.note: to hare is to run very fast, so hares means speeds
a foot is a metrical unit, one section of a line of verse

explanation.surface: A wild flower rushes through a stanza.
explanation.definitionFit: Hare's-foot is a wild clover with soft furry flower heads, named for their likeness to a hare's paw.

clue.text: Trim beard, fine one

parts.note: F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
an ace is the one in a suit of cards

explanation.surface: A barber offers to tidy a customer's beard, and a good job it is too.
explanation.walkthrough: Two meanings of the word come first, then wordplay for it: fine plus one. 'Trim beard' reads as one instruction, but the two words are separate definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: To face a garment is to trim its edge with facing material, and to face someone is to confront or beard them.

clue.text: Sigh maybe as Special gets involved in rule over Ireland?

indicators.note: something involved in a thing is caught up inside it, so the abbreviation goes within the country name

parts.note: R is an abbreviation for rule
Eire is the Irish name for Ireland; its first letter
SP is the abbreviation for special

explanation.surface: A sigh, perhaps, at special forces deployed to impose rule on Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' puts R above the rest: R + E(SP)IRE. 'Sigh maybe' is a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: To respire is to breathe, and a sigh is one particular kind of breath, hence 'maybe'.

clue.text: Language, one that's taught in school but not at work

parts.note: the ling is a fish, and fish swim in schools: a joke on being taught at school
O marks the off position on a switch, the state of anything not working

explanation.surface: A foreign language is something you learn in the classroom but never use in your job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'School' suggests a classroom; it is a school of fish. This parse is the annotator's best reading of the second half.
explanation.definitionFit: Lingo is an informal word for a language, especially a foreign one or a specialist jargon.

clue.text: 'Dark lady' for Shakespeare to court — disappointment follows

parts.note: to woo is to court a lover
a sell is a let-down or hoax, as in 'what a sell!'

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's mysterious Dark Lady of the sonnets is wooed, and he is let down.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dark Lady of Shakespeare's sonnets is a red herring: the answer is his spelling of ouzel, the blackbird, so a dark lady is a female blackbird.
explanation.definitionFit: Woosel is Shakespeare's form of ouzel, the blackbird, as in 'the woosel cock so black of hue', a dark-feathered bird.

clue.text: Runner, once unpredictable

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a skid or runner, as under a sledge
second meaning: an obsolete adjective for slippery and untrustworthy

explanation.surface: A former athlete was erratic in form.
explanation.definitionFit: A slipper is a skid on which something slides, and as an old adjective it meant slippery, hence not to be relied on.

clue.text: Paintings to preserve with containers

parts.note: to can food is to preserve it in tins
vases are containers for flowers

explanation.surface: Works of art are being stored away with some pots for safe keeping.
explanation.definitionFit: Oil paintings are made on canvas, so a canvas is a common name for one picture.

clue.text: 'Tar-clad' etc, this could be cleanly extracted

definitions.text: 'Tar-clad' etc, this could be cleanly extracted

indicators.note: says the letters of the phrase could be rearranged into this answer plus the named words

parts.note: the composite fodder, whose letters hold the answer together with TARCLAD and ETC

explanation.surface: A chemist muses that tarry stuff could be drawn off neatly.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the letters of 'cleanly extracted' are those of 'Tar-clad' and 'etc' plus 'this', the answer. Remove TARCLADETC and the six letters left make the hydrocarbon.
explanation.definitionFit: Xylene is an aromatic hydrocarbon obtained from coal tar, so it is indeed extracted from tar.

clue.text: US novel, fifth print?

parts.note: type is printed lettering
E is the fifth letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: A query about the fifth printing of an American book.
explanation.definitionFit: Typee was Herman Melville's first novel, a South Seas adventure, an American work of fiction.

clue.text: Trader's seductive plan: spot includes devious shtick mostly (13, two words)

indicators.note: the spot holds the scrambled letters within it

parts.note: a swelling is a spot or pimple on the skin

indicators.note: devious suggests twisting, so the letters are rearranged
mostly means all but the last letter is used

explanation.surface: A salesman's slick pitch: a pimple complete with a twisty routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spot' reads as noticing, but it is a pimple; shtick is a comedian's routine.
explanation.definitionFit: Switch selling is the sales trick of luring customers with a cheap offer and then steering them to a pricier item.

clue.text: Large stinger? Drunk another, first polished off

indicators.note: a drunk person staggers about, so the letters reel into a new order
to polish something off is to finish it, so the opening letter is done away with

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A big cocktail in a bar; the drinker sank another and finished the first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stinger' is the name of a cocktail, which suits the drinking surface, but here it is an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: The hornet is the largest European wasp, and its sting is notoriously painful, so it is a large stinging insect.

clue.text: E.g. pea stick stuck in meadow

indicators.note: the adhesive word is lodged within the field word

parts.note: lee is given in Chambers as a variant spelling of lea, a meadow
gum is glue, something used to stick

explanation.surface: A pea-stick pushed into a grassy field, as in a vegetable patch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pea stick' reads as a garden cane, but the definition stops at 'pea', and 'stick' is the glue.
explanation.definitionFit: The pea is a typical member of the bean family of pod-bearing plants, so it is an example of the answer.

clue.text: Clothing ultimate in tastelessness, dull and dowdy

definitions.note: a noun here: a dowdy, frumpish woman

indicators.note: clothing something covers it all round, so the word for dull is wrapped round the letter

parts.note: mopy means dull and listless; its first three letters
the last letter of mopy

indicators.note: the ultimate thing is the last one, so only the final letter of the next word is used

parts.note: the final letter of tastelessness

explanation.surface: Someone's outfit is the last word in bad taste: drab and frumpy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dowdy' reads as an adjective, but the definition is a noun, a dowdy woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A mopsy is an old word for a frump, a shabbily or untidily dressed woman.

clue.text: Designs requirement for comfortable life

definitions.meaning: first meaning: intends or plans, a verb
second meaning: money, the resources one lives on

explanation.surface: Plans are what is needed to live in comfort.
explanation.definitionFit: To mean something is to intend it, and a person of means has enough money to live comfortably.

clue.text: Rand maybe in south-eastern state discontinued

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it, so the novelist's first name goes within the compass points

parts.note: SE is the abbreviation for south-eastern; its first letter
Ayn Rand was the Russian-American novelist; 'maybe' marks Rand as one bearer of the first name

explanation.surface: The South African currency, the rand, perhaps in a south-eastern state that no longer exists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rand' looks like the South African currency; it is the writer Ayn Rand. 'State' is a verb, not a country.
explanation.definitionFit: Sayne is an obsolete infinitive of say, so it is a word for state that has fallen out of use.

clue.text: String in past times run up to make baseball equipment

indicators.note: in a down clue, running upward means reading from the bottom, so the letters are turned round
a string of letters in a phrase is a run of them sitting inside it, spanning the word gap

parts.note: the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Some cord from an earlier era is sewn up into gear for a ball game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'String' looks like cord and 'run up' like sewing, but a string here is a run of letters, and in a down clue 'run up' turns them round.
explanation.definitionFit: Mitts are the padded gloves baseball catchers and first basemen wear, part of a player's kit.

clue.text: Showing reluctance that shaver seldom admits

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so the words before it let the answer in across their join

parts.note: the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A man rarely reaches for his razor because he cannot be bothered.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone averse to a thing dislikes it and is unwilling to do it, so is reluctant.

clue.text: Chopper makes basic calculation for those listening

indicators.note: for listeners the word is heard rather than seen, so its sound is what counts

parts.note: adds is the simplest arithmetic, putting numbers together

explanation.surface: A helicopter does simple arithmetic for an audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chopper' suggests a helicopter, but it is a cutting tool.
explanation.definitionFit: An adze is a cutting tool with an arched blade at right angles to the handle, used for chopping and shaping wood.

clue.text: Festival? Take time out for one offering relaxation

indicators.note: taking something out removes it, so the letter for time comes out of the festival

parts.note: Easter is the Christian spring festival
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A holiday advertised as time off for someone who needs to unwind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take time out' reads as advice to rest, which fits the festival; here it removes one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An easer is something or someone that eases, bringing relief or relaxation.

clue.text: Ancient aristocrat, wildly irate about rising, died

indicators.note: the scrambled letters go about, that is around, the word for rising
wildly suggests letters thrown around, so irate is rearranged

parts.note: up means rising, as in 'the sun is up'
D is the genealogical abbreviation for died

explanation.surface: An old nobleman, fuming as he got up, then passed away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' looks like a reversal signal, but it is simply a synonym. A Eupatrid belonged to the noble families of ancient Athens.
explanation.definitionFit: A Eupatrid was a member of the hereditary aristocracy of ancient Athens.

clue.text: Passage (small) or one end of it?

parts.note: the opening letter of passage
taken as written
it is the passage, and this is its other end

explanation.surface: Is the answer a small passage, or just one end of one?
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer aloud as letters: P or E, the two ends of the word passage. The clue spells its own answer while defining it.
explanation.definitionFit: A pore is a tiny opening in skin or rock through which fluid can pass, so a minute passage.

clue.text: A governor, industrious one temporarily inactive

parts.note: taken as written
a bey was a Turkish provincial governor
the ant is proverbially hard-working

explanation.surface: A hard-working governor has been suspended from duty for a while.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, an abeyant right or estate is in abeyance, held in suspension until it is claimed, so dormant for now.

clue.text: Where students gather, almost half intoxicated over liqueurs

parts.note: the OU is the Open University, Britain's distance-learning university

indicators.note: turned over means flipped round, so the remaining letters read in the opposite order
almost half means a little less than half, so most of the word is cut away

parts.note: sozzled is British slang for drunk

explanation.surface: Students at a university bar, half-drunk, are knocking back liqueurs.
explanation.walkthrough: SOZZLED has seven letters; its first three, a little under half, are turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Ouzo is a Greek aniseed-flavoured spirit, often drunk as an aperitif, here in the plural.

clue.text: Foppish dresser (50s style) returned fur, showing resolve

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the letters read backwards

parts.note: a Ted, or Teddy boy, was a 1950s British youth in Edwardian-style clothes
ermine is the white winter fur of the stoat

explanation.surface: A dandy in 1950s gear sent back a fur coat, a sign of determination.
explanation.definitionFit: To determine is to decide firmly, the same as to resolve on a course of action.

clue.text: Council vehicle? Dodging tester, one patrolling boundary (13, two words)

indicators.note: dodging means moving shiftily from side to side, so the letters shift about

parts.note: taken as written
in cricket a sweeper is a fielder posted out by the boundary rope to cut off fours

explanation.surface: A council van dodges the inspector while a guard patrols the perimeter.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that the answer may be a person as well as a cleaning lorry run by the local council.
explanation.definitionFit: A street sweeper is a road-cleaning vehicle operated by local councils, the bodies responsible for keeping streets clean.
